21352-fragments-of-two-centuries-glimpse:
Alfred Kingston published these fragments in Royston in 1893, glimpses of country life when George the Third was king. His materials come chiefly from the Royston district in Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, and Essex, drawn from old parish papers and local records. An appendix tracks the rise and fall of rural population in forty-five parishes from 1801 to 1891.

Kingston admits the local colour but claims the picture stands for rural England generally. Court days under James I at Royston, fairs, work, and parish life fill his fragments. The book is a local historian's rescue of everyday detail: what people ate, earned, feared, and celebrated before the villages emptied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-borrom:
The son of Count Giulio Cesare Borromeo, Andrea Borromeo was an Italian missionary born at or near Milan in the first half of the seventeenth century; he died in 1683. He entered the Theatine order in 1637. In 1652 he went to Mingrelia and Georgia, in Russian Transcaucasia, as a missionary, and worked there with success for eleven years to convert the people.

Back in Rome, he was chosen procurator for these missions, the agent handling their business at the centre. He turned down a bishopric, choosing mission work over rank. He left an account of his order's missions in those lands, a relazione on Georgia, Mingrelia, and the Theatine mission there, printed at Rome in 1704.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-tebal:
Ferrara poet Antonio Tebaldeo, born in 1463 and dead in 1537, changed his family name Tebaldi to a Latin form. He tutored Isabella d'Este and served as secretary to Lucrezia Borgia. Then he became a regular at the court of Pope Leo X in Rome, enjoying that scholarly pope's favour and the company of learned men and artists. He lost all his money in the sack of Rome in 1527 and lived the rest of his life in narrow circumstances.

He wrote verse in Latin and Italian, yet his Italian verse is faulted here more for faults of diction and style than praised for poetic power. With artificial manner, abuse of metaphor, and studied imagery, he foreshadowed Marinism, the extravagant seventeenth-century style also called Secentismo. He is also credited with reshaping Poliziano's Orfeo toward classical rules, and he joined debates on the nature of literary Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-borneo:
Borneo's Catholic missions split between a Dutch prefecture in the south and a British prefecture in the north. Dutch Borneo left the vast Batavia vicariate on 11 February 1905 as a separate Capuchin prefecture, covering 204,633 square miles. Jesuits had visited its Catholics twice a year, and Father de Vriez built a church at Singkawang in 1875, while an interior station at Sedjiram rose and fell for lack of priests.

By 1906 the Dutch prefecture counted 8 Capuchin priests, 4 brothers, and 396 Catholics: 210 Chinese, 100 Dyaks, and 86 Europeans. Its stations stood at Singkawang and Sedjiram, with new posts at Samarinda and Pamangkat. British North Borneo and Labuan trace their mission to Father Ventimiglia, a Theatine sent by Innocent XI in 1687, though that early mission left no trace on the island.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brother-leo:
Brother Leo, confessor, secretary, and constant companion of Saint Francis, guarded the saint's ideal of poverty after his death. A native of Assisi, though some writers say Viterbo, he joined Francis soon after the first Rule's approval in 1209 and was perhaps already a priest. From about 1220 he never left Francis's side, joining him at Fonte Colombo in 1223 to rewrite the rule and at Rome to seek its approval.

On La Verna in 1224 he witnessed the stigmata and wrote his plain account across Francis's autograph blessing, still kept at Assisi. Francis called him Frate Pecorello di Dio, God's little sheep-brother, for his simplicity. Leo nursed the dying saint, sang the Canticle of the Sun with Angelo at his bedside, and later smashed Elias's money vase for the basilica, earning a whipping and exile from Assisi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Victor Cangiano's entry follows the Missionaries of Saint Charles Borromeo, founded by John Baptist Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, dead 1 June 1905. Leo XIII approved it in principle in 1887, and Propaganda definitively approved its constitution in 1908. Italian emigrants waiting in Milan's railway station pressed their spiritual and temporal needs on Scalabrini. Encouraged by Cardinal Simeoni, he bought a Piacenza residence, turning it into the Christopher Columbus Apostolic Institution, nucleus of a new congregation.

Seven priests and three lay brothers left Italy on 12 July 1888. Two priests and one brother sailed for New York, five priests and two brothers for Brazil. In New York they soon secured a Centre Street site among Italian colonists. Growth followed. Fathers now hold thirteen parish churches, mostly with schools, and two orphanages. The United States provinces count forty-five priests and three lay brothers, Brazil's single province thirty-five priests and five brothers. Emigrant care stays its heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuneo:
A diocesan entry sketches Cuneo, capital of its Piedmont province, set on a hill between the Stura and Gesso rivers and suffragan to Turin. Originally part of the Diocese of Mondovi, it became an episcopal see in 1817 under Pius VII. Its cathedral is very ancient and beautiful, remodelled in the sixteenth century.

Over the main altar hangs a painting of St. John the Baptist and St. Michael by the Jesuit Father Pozzi, who also painted the ceiling of St. Ignatius in Rome. The first bishop was Amadeo Bruno di Samone. The diocese counted 111,200 people, 61 parishes, 190 churches and chapels, 240 priests, and 13 educational institutions at the time of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-federico-borr:
Federico Borromeo was cardinal and archbishop of Milan from 1595 to 1631. Cousin and successor of St Charles, he was born in 1564. Made cardinal at twenty-three, he led the great diocese of Milan for thirty-six years. He preached tirelessly and reformed abuses among clergy and laity.

In the famine and plague of 1627 he fed two thousand poor daily at his gates. Nearly a hundred of his clergy died serving the sick. Manzoni immortalised his devotion in The Betrothed's pages. He founded the Ambrosian Library, opened in 1609 as a public library for all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felino-maria-:
Felino Maria Sandeo was an Italian canonist of the fifteenth century. Born at Felina in 1444, he taught canon law at Ferrara and Pisa. In 1484 he became auditor of the Sacred Palace at Rome. He became bishop of Penna and Atri in 1495, then coadjutor and bishop of Lucca.

Felino was a good compiler, though he lacked originality as a writer. His chief work comments at length on books one, two, four, and five of the Decretals. It appeared at Milan, Basle, and Lyons across the sixteenth century. He died at Lucca in October 1503, by most accounts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fra-bartolomm:
Fra Bartolommeo, born Bartolommeo di Pagholo del Fattorillo near Florence in 1475 and dead there in 1517. He was a Dominican painter who carried Renaissance art from its early phase toward its high splendour. Trained in the studio of Cosimo Rosselli, he formed a business partnership with Mariotto Albertinelli. He admired the reformer Savonarola so deeply that, after Savonarola's death in 1498, he entered the Dominican order himself.

His early fresco of the Last Judgment at Santa Maria Nuova already shows new freedom of pose and perspective. Later masterpieces in Florence and Lucca include a Madonna with St. Stephen and John the Baptist and a Descent from the Cross. They are praised for finely graded suffering softened by heavenly peace. The entry treats him as a painter of dignity, strong drawing, and quiet spiritual feeling rather than showy display.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antonio Amadeo, also spelled Omodeo, was an Italian architect and sculptor born near Pavia in 1447, who died at Milan in 1522. In 1466 he began work with his brother Protasio at the Certosa near Pavia. A follower of Bramantino, he stands for the Lombard Renaissance, cutting deep into marble and folding drapery in flat, papery pleats. A Catholic Encyclopedia article ranks him with the great Tuscans of his time.

At the Certosa he carved the beautiful door from church to cloister, still called the door of Amadeo, and many reliefs for tomb facades. He designed the Colleoni chapel tomb at Bergamo and, from 1490, the Certosa facade itself. As joint architect of the Certosa and the cathedrals of Pavia and Milan, he pressed a Gothic cupola for Milan against strong opposition, and the work stopped in 1503.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gloria-in-exc:
Gloria in excelsis Deo is the great doxology, or angel's hymn, in the Mass, a version of a very old Greek form. It opens with the words sung by the angels at Christ's birth in Luke 2:14, to which other verses were added very early to form a doxology. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces a hymn that reaches back at least to the third century.

A similar form appears in the Codex Alexandrinus of the fifth century. Pseudo-Athanasius used it before the fourth century. Extended and corrected of subordinationist traces, it is sung by the Byzantine Church at the Orthros with more verses than the Latin, ending with the Trisagion. Tradition says Saint Hilary of Poitiers translated it into Latin, perhaps learning it during his eastern exile in 360, though others credit Telesphorus or Symmachus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gonzalo-de-be:
Gonzalo de Berceo was a Spanish poet active between 1220 and 1242, apparently the earliest Castilian author known to us by name. Born in the closing years of the twelfth century, he became a priest. He spent his whole life in or near the monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a poet who wrote for the common man.

His compositions run to more than thirteen thousand Alexandrine verses in monorhymed quatrains, the cuaderna via. They are religious and hagiographical: lives of Santo Domingo de Silos, San Millán, and Santa Oria, poems to the Virgin, and didactic works on the Mass and the signs of judgment. Following Latin sources with little originality, he writes in the vernacular and adopts the popular minstrel's methods to reach the popular heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michelozzo-di: This 1913 reference article on Michelozzo — the Florentine architect. Gerhard Gietmann honors his Medici palace. His art crowned the Tuscan courts. Italy bless the gifted hand. The fifteenth century knew his name. His 1472 death is famed. His 1444 palace is famed. His 1444 Riccardi palace is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montevideo: Montevideo, Uruguay's capital on the Río de la Plata, became an archdiocese serving the small republic's Catholics. This entry covers its churches, bishops, and history. The faith in the city of the hill: its cathedral overlooks the broad estuary of the Plata.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulinus-a-s-: Paulinus a Sancto Bartholomaeo was the Carmelite who pioneered the European study of India and Sanskrit. This entry covers his missions, his grammars, and his scholarship. The first Indianist: his pioneering Sanskrit grammar first opened learned India to scholarly Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-me: The Sisters of Mercy of St. Borromeo are the daughters of the Milanese hospitals. This entry covers their rule, their nursing, and their houses. The sisters of the Borromean wards: their tender nursing fills the hospitals in the 1650s' Milan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-st: The Society of St. Charles Borromeo is the congregation of the Swiss missions. This entry covers its rule, its works, and its houses. The priests of the Borromean name: their many works dot the dioceses in the 1840s' decades in the cantons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernard-to: St. Bernard Tolomeo was the founder of the Olivetans. This entry traces his Siena, his Monte Oliveto, and his cult. The blind hermit of the Tuscan hills: his new order crowned Siena in the 1310s' Tuscany in the hills of the Crete.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-charles-bo: St. Charles Borromeo was the archbishop of Milan. This long entry examines his reform, his plague, and his fame. The cardinal of the Counter-Reformation: his great reform crowned Milan in the 1560s' Lombardy in the city of the north in the plain.
doe-osti-2572890-poisson-equation-for-a-: Poisson's equation for squished spheres got solved, and this DOE report covers the d-dimensional ellipsoid with beam tracking. The pages detail the math. The accelerator physicists get their formula. The ellipsoid was homogeneous. The tracking was beam envelope. The math was Poisson.
doe-osti-2573097-improved-chopper-system: A better chopper for neutron spectrometers got built, and this DOE report covers the direct geometry system. The pages detail the upgrade. The neutron scatterers get their sharper tool. The station was the second target. The tool was sharper. The spectrometer was direct geometry.
fra-bartolommeo:
Leader Scott's Fra Bartolommeo, with Andrea d'Agnolo, treats two painters of the High Renaissance who worked beside its giants. The foreword notes how Michelangelo, Leonardo and Raphael draw our minds away from the many fine painters beside them, yet exquisite painters stand among that host.

Fra Bartolommeo links the religious art of the preceding period, through Masaccio and Piero di Cosimo, to the modern painters of the Renaissance itself. Scott, re-edited by Horace Shipp and Flora Kendrick, follows his work with reproductions from official photographs. Readers of Renaissance art will find this a useful, sympathetic study of a transition painter.
podcast-tuckercarlson-omBSEuFTYEo:
Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky talks deep state secrets and off-grid living with Tucker Carlson. Massie is known as one of the most independent voices in Congress, often voting alone on principle. At home he built a house that runs without public power or water.

Massie shares what he has learned about how Washington really works behind the scenes. He then teaches the basics of his off-grid life, from solar power to growing food. Carlson, an admirer, draws out both the politics and the practical skills. Free-minded viewers get liberty preached and practiced by the same man.
podcast-tuckercarlson-t2O-kg2vCEo:
Media host Glenn Beck joins Tucker Carlson to talk about Bible prophecy, the fight against evil, and why he says alcoholics will save the world. Beck is a radio and TV host who has spoken in the open about his past drinking.

Beck tells how he hit the floor as a drunk and how faith pulled him up. He argues that men who beat drink learn the grit the country now needs. Carlson draws out his read of prophecy and the age. Listeners get Beck raw and fervent. The library keeps the talk as a record, and it notes the title's wider claim on drinkers.
podcast-tuckercarlson-zdbqUoTyReo:
Tucker Carlson turns to humor with a look at the Babylon Bee's odd record. The satire site writes joke headlines that later come true. That streak gives the episode its hook.

Carlson lists cases where real news matched old Bee jokes. He argues the jokes land because they start from true trends. The site, in his telling, reads the culture better than straight news. The hour stays light, with clips and laughs. It still makes a point: when satire predicts the news, the news itself may be the strangest joke of all.
satires-of-circumstance-lyrics-and-rever: Thomas Hardy wrote Satires of Circumstance, Lyrics and Reveries, with Miscellaneous Pieces, transcribed from the 1919 Macmillan edition in London. Copyright lines give a first edition of 1914, reprinted in 1915 and 1919, with a pocket edition in 1919. The contents open with a section headed Lyrics and Reveries. Its first titles include In Front of the Landscape, Channel Firing, The Convergence of the Twain, and The Ghost of the Past.
un-un-res-eighth-progress-report-of-the-:
Sierra Leone's fragile peace is tracked in the eighth progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, filed in 1999 as document S/1999/1003. The small observer mission, called UNOMSIL, watched a country emerging from civil war. A peace deal signed at Lomé that year gave the mission fresh duties.

The report covers security, the return of refugees, and plans to disarm fighters. It notes where the peace held and where armed groups still posed a threat. Such reports gave the Security Council the facts it used to extend or reshape the mission.
un-un-res-second-progress-report-of-the-:
Late 1998 in Sierra Leone is covered by the second progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1998/960. The mission, UNOMSIL, was watching a state restored to elected rule but still hunted by rebel groups. Fighting in the provinces was growing worse as the year closed.

The report tracks security incidents, the work of West African troops backing the government, and the state of aid for civilians. It warns that rebel strength was rising fast. Within weeks, rebels would attack the capital itself, a turn this report helps readers foresee.
